options: Not yet. Naloxone wears off in 30–60 minutes, before morphine does. Keep him monitored for at least 2 hours after the last naloxone dose (longer is safer with morphine and poor kidneys), ask the primary anaesthetist whether he needs a monitored bed (their decision), avoid more morphine, and record everything.
Send him to the ward with a dose of naloxone written up in case.
Yes: he is awake and strong now.
questions.explain:
The danger is the naloxone wearing off while the morphine is still working. Watch him long enough, and leave the monitored-bed decision to a senior.

The other choices:
• “Send him to the ward with a dose of naloxone written up in case.” A dose written up only helps if someone notices in time. He needs watching where staff can see him, for at least 2 hours after his last naloxone.
• “Yes: he is awake and strong now.” Naloxone lasts less than an hour; in kidney disease morphine’s effects last much longer.
questions.source: MO guide case: PACU: drowsy and breathing slowly (pacu-drowsy), step 5

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.

What do you do first?
options: One day off is close enough: carry on.
Pin down the facts: the exact drugs, doses and time of the last doses (ask him, check the ward chart), and his kidney function. Then plan to call your consultant today.
Tell him the operation is cancelled.
questions.explain:
Facts first. Your consultant will want the exact time of the last doses and his kidney function before deciding anything.

The other choices:
• “One day off is close enough: carry on.” It isn’t close. Apixaban taken this morning will still be working tomorrow, and the timing decides whether a spinal is safe. Flag it.
• “Tell him the operation is cancelled.” Not your decision. The department rule: don’t cancel or refer cases on your own. Get the facts, then call your consultant.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 1

questions.stem:
Last apixaban 5 mg at 08:00 today, and empagliflozin 10 mg at the same time. His kidney function is normal. Your consultant may plan a spinal. What is the key point about the apixaban?

The case so far: A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.
options: He needs enoxaparin bridging while the apixaban is stopped.

The time of the last dose. By tomorrow morning it will be only about 24 hours: short of the handbook’s 2 days for surgery, and a spinal needs a longer gap still. Your consultant decides with the surgeon: usually postpone.
Let him take tonight’s dose as usual and sort it out tomorrow.
questions.explain:
Yes. The handbook’s 2 days is the general surgical timing (longer when the kidneys are poor); spinals and epidurals need a longer, separate interval, set out in [the spinal page’s table](../../spinal/#tq-anticoag). Give your consultant the exact time and his kidney function.

The other choices:
• “He needs enoxaparin bridging while the apixaban is stopped.” Apixaban and the other direct oral anticoagulants don’t need bridging: they wear off and start working quickly. Bridging is for some patients on warfarin, and it is the consultant’s and surgeon’s decision.
• “Let him take tonight’s dose as usual and sort it out tomorrow.” Tonight’s dose would push the safe time for surgery or a spinal back even further. This needs a decision tonight, from your consultant.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 2

questions.stem:
The empagliflozin: he took it this morning. His glucose today is 7.8 mmol/L.

The case so far: A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.

Which is the best choice?
options: Stop his metformin too and start an insulin infusion tonight.
No problem: his glucose is normal.

Flag it. SGLT2 inhibitors (the “-gliflozins”) should stop 3 days before surgery because of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Omit it from now, ask for ketones and glucose to be checked on the morning, and let your consultant decide whether the case can go ahead.
questions.explain:
Right. These drugs can cause ketoacidosis with a normal glucose, especially when fasting and stressed by surgery. Ketones, not glucose, show it.

The other choices:
• “Stop his metformin too and start an insulin infusion tonight.” Diabetes medicine plans follow the department guideline and your consultant; an overnight insulin infusion isn’t needed for this. Flag it rather than improvising.
• “No problem: his glucose is normal.” That is the trap: euglycaemic DKA happens with a normal glucose. Ketones show it, not glucose.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 3

questions.stem:
He snores loudly, is tired in the day, and his wife has seen him stop breathing at night. Neck 44 cm. He was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and given a CPAP machine, but rarely uses it.

The case so far: A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.

Which is the best choice?
options: OSA is common: nothing to do.
Book a high dependency (HD) bed yourself.

STOP-BANG 7/8 with known OSA. Ask him to use his CPAP tonight and bring it tomorrow, and flag it to your consultant: an opioid-sparing plan, and whether he needs a monitored bed afterwards (their decision).
questions.explain:
Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoeas, high blood Pressure, Age over 50, Neck over 40 cm, male Gender: 7 of 8 (his BMI is just under 35). Bringing the CPAP and an opioid-sparing plan both make the night after surgery safer.

The other choices:
• “OSA is common: nothing to do.” Untreated OSA makes him sensitive to opioids and sedatives and more likely to obstruct after surgery. It changes the plan, so flag it.
• “Book a high dependency (HD) bed yourself.” Checking HD or ICU needs is part of a premed, but whether he needs a bed is your consultant’s call. Flag it and ask.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 4

questions.stem:
His airway: Mallampati 3, thyromental distance 6 cm, mouth opening 3 fingers, full neck movement, and a loose upper front tooth.

The case so far: A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.

Which is the best choice?
options: Pull the loose tooth out yourself so it can’t fall into the airway.
It’s only one tooth: not worth mentioning.
Document it, warn him that the tooth could be damaged or come out during airway management, record that you told him, and tell your consultant.
questions.explain:
Dental damage is one of the commonest complaints after an anaesthetic. A documented, counselled loose tooth is a known risk; an unmentioned one is a surprise for everyone.

The other choices:
• “Pull the loose tooth out yourself so it can’t fall into the airway.” Not your job, and not without a dentist. Document it, counsel him and tell your consultant.
• “It’s only one tooth: not worth mentioning.” Loose teeth can be knocked out by a laryngoscope or a bite block, and could be inhaled. Counsel him, document it and tell your consultant.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 5

questions.stem:
You call your consultant. What do you say?

The case so far: A 64-year-old man, 98 kg, 170 cm (BMI 34), is first on tomorrow’s list for a left total knee replacement. The pre-op clinic notes: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) on metformin and empagliflozin; atrial fibrillation on apixaban; hypertension; “told to stop apixaban 2 days and empagliflozin 3 days before surgery.” He tells you he took both this morning: no one told him to stop.
options: Send a message with the main points, and leave the apixaban for the morning team to sort out.

“First case tomorrow: 64-year-old man for a left knee replacement, BMI 34. Three problems. One: he took apixaban and empagliflozin at 08:00 today; nobody told him to stop. Two: OSA, STOP-BANG 7, rarely uses CPAP; I’ve asked him to bring it. Three: loose upper front tooth, Mallampati 3. Diabetes with HbA1c 8.2 on metformin; kidneys normal. What would you like me to do?”
Call the surgeon and tell them to cancel.
questions.explain:
Short, numbered, with the facts that matter and a clear question at the end. Your consultant can decide in one call.

The other choices:
• “Send a message with the main points, and leave the apixaban for the morning team to sort out.” A message is better than nothing, but the anticoagulant timing needs a decision tonight. Call, don’t just text, when something affects whether the case goes ahead.
• “Call the surgeon and tell them to cancel.” Not your decision to make or pass on. Your consultant decides, and speaks to the surgeon.
questions.source: MO guide case: A premed with several problems (premed-flags), step 6

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”

What do you do first?
options: A rapid sequence induction (RSI): he isn’t fasted and has an acute abdomen, so he is at high risk of aspiration.
Wait until he has been fasted for 6 hours.
A standard induction with a supraglottic airway: it’s a short case.
questions.explain:
Both are on the handbook’s list of reasons for an RSI: inadequate fasting and an acute abdomen.

The other choices:
• “Wait until he has been fasted for 6 hours.” Pain, opioids and the inflamed appendix slow the stomach, so it may still be full at 6 hours, and delay risks perforation. Treat him as a full stomach whatever the clock says.
• “A standard induction with a supraglottic airway: it’s a short case.” A supraglottic airway doesn’t protect the lungs from vomit. Inadequate fasting and an acute abdomen both call for an RSI.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 1

questions.stem:
Your consultant agrees an RSI with propofol and suxamethonium. What do you prepare?

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”
options: Draw up the induction drugs, and fetch extra kit only if there’s a problem.
Propofol and rocuronium 45 mg (0.6 mg/kg).

Doses worked out and drawn up: propofol 150 mg (2 mg/kg; your consultant gives less if his BP is low or he looks septic) and suxamethonium 100 mg (1–1.5 mg/kg of total body weight), with rocuronium and sugammadex available. Suction on and under the pillow; bougie, video laryngoscope, a smaller tube and a second-generation supraglottic airway ready; the AU nurse briefed on cricoid pressure.
questions.explain:
Everything ready before you start: in an RSI there is no time to fetch anything.

The other choices:
• “Draw up the induction drugs, and fetch extra kit only if there’s a problem.” In an RSI there is no time to fetch kit. Everything must be ready, checked and within reach before you start.
• “Propofol and rocuronium 45 mg (0.6 mg/kg).” 0.6 mg/kg is the routine intubating dose and takes 2–3 minutes. For an RSI rocuronium is 1–1.2 mg/kg so that it works in about a minute: about 75–90 mg for him. (The handbook says 1 mg/kg of lean body weight, which under-doses a man who isn’t obese; in obesity your consultant chooses the weight.) And your consultant chose suxamethonium.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 2

questions.stem:
He is on the table with monitors on. How do you preoxygenate and position him?

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”
options: Thirty seconds of oxygen: speed matters in an RSI.

Head up about 20–30°, a tight-fitting mask with 100% oxygen for 3 minutes of normal breathing until the EtO2 is above 80% (the handbook’s minimum; aim for 90% or more). The AU nurse presses lightly on the cricoid (10 N) while he is awake and firmly (30 N) as he goes to sleep.
Firm cricoid pressure from the start, while he is awake.
questions.explain:
Head-up preoxygenation fills the lungs with more oxygen and buys apnoea time. Cricoid pressure goes from light to firm as he loses consciousness.

The other choices:
• “Thirty seconds of oxygen: speed matters in an RSI.” Speed matters after induction, not before. Full preoxygenation buys the time you will need if intubation is difficult.
• “Firm cricoid pressure from the start, while he is awake.” 30 N on an awake patient hurts and can make him retch. Light pressure while awake, firm as consciousness goes.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 3

questions.stem:
EtO2 92%. Your consultant gives propofol 150 mg then suxamethonium 100 mg in quick succession, with cricoid pressure on. Fasciculations ripple across his chest. Your consultant: “You do the laryngoscopy.”

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”

Which is the best choice?
options: Bag him firmly while you wait for the suxamethonium.
Start the laryngoscopy at once, during the fasciculations.
Don’t bag. Wait until the fasciculations stop (about 45–60 seconds), then laryngoscopy. If he desaturates, gentle mask ventilation (no more than 20 cmH2O) is your consultant’s call.
questions.explain:
The handbook: no bagging until the tube is confirmed. Current practice allows gentle mask ventilation during an RSI if the saturation falls; your consultant decides.

The other choices:
• “Bag him firmly while you wait for the suxamethonium.” Firm bagging fills the stomach with gas and makes vomiting more likely: exactly what an RSI is designed to avoid.
• “Start the laryngoscopy at once, during the fasciculations.” Wait for the fasciculations to finish: until then the jaw and cords may not be relaxed.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 4

questions.stem:
You look: you can see only the epiglottis, no cords and no arytenoids (Cormack–Lehane grade 3). SpO2 98%.

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”

Which is the best choice?
options: Say what you see (“Grade 3, no cords”), take the blade out and hand over to your consultant, with the bougie and video laryngoscope ready. Your consultant may ask the nurse to ease the cricoid.
Keep trying with the same blade for another minute.
Pass the tube blindly where you think the cords are.
questions.explain:
Saying it early lets the most experienced person make the next attempt with the right kit, while the saturation is still good.

The other choices:
• “Keep trying with the same blade for another minute.” A long attempt with a poor view uses up his oxygen and causes swelling. Repeating the same thing rarely gives a different result.
• “Pass the tube blindly where you think the cords are.” Blind attempts often go into the oesophagus and cause swelling and bleeding.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 5

questions.stem:
Your consultant passes a bougie using the video laryngoscope and slides a size 8.0 tube over it. The cuff is inflated.

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”

Which is the best choice?
options: The SpO2 is rising, so it’s in: release the cricoid.
Release the cricoid as soon as the tube passes the cords.
Confirm with a sustained capnography trace, chest rise and listening on both sides. Cricoid pressure comes off only after that.
questions.explain:
Right. The cricoid stays on until the cuff is up and the tube is confirmed in the trachea.

The other choices:
• “The SpO2 is rising, so it’s in: release the cricoid.” Saturation can rise briefly even with a misplaced tube. Sustained capnography first, then release.
• “Release the cricoid as soon as the tube passes the cords.” Keep it on until the cuff is inflated and capnography confirms the tube is in the trachea.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 6

questions.stem:
Surgery goes well. At the end your consultant asks how he should be woken up.

The case so far: A 28-year-old man, 75 kg, 175 cm, for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He ate a full meal 3 hours ago, has vomited once and still feels sick. Temperature 38.1 °C. His airway assessment is normal. Your consultant: “How shall we put him to sleep?”

Which is the best choice?
options: Extubate deep, to avoid coughing.
Extubate him yourself while your consultant starts the next case.
Empty the stomach through an orogastric tube, make sure the block is fully reversed (TOF ratio over 0.9), and extubate with your consultant once he is fully awake, obeying commands and sitting up.
questions.explain:
A full-stomach patient needs his protective reflexes back before the tube comes out: fully awake and sitting up.

The other choices:
• “Extubate deep, to avoid coughing.” A deep extubation leaves an unprotected airway in a full-stomach patient. He needs his reflexes back: fully awake.
• “Extubate him yourself while your consultant starts the next case.” In your first month you never extubate or end a case alone: call, then wait.
questions.source: MO guide case: RSI for an appendicectomy (rsi-appendix), step 7

questions.stem:
A 76-year-old man, 70 kg, with hypertension, is having a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) under spinal anaesthesia. Your consultant gave 2.5 mL of 0.5% heavy bupivacaine at L3–4. He is in lithotomy, and your consultant has gone to the control room, asking you to check the BP every 2–3 minutes. At your consultant’s request, phenylephrine and ephedrine are drawn up and labelled. Six minutes after the spinal he says, “I feel sick.” He looks pale and sweaty.

What do you do first?
options: Nausea after a spinal means low blood pressure until proven otherwise: give ephedrine 5 mg IV now and repeat in 2–3 minutes if needed, give oxygen, and ask the nurse to call your consultant.
Give an antiemetic for the nausea.
Phenylephrine 100 mcg IV.
Wait for the next BP reading.
questions.explain:
The spinal blocks the sympathetic nerves, so the vessels widen and the BP falls. Nausea is often the first sign. With a slow heart rate, ephedrine is a good choice.

The other choices:
• “Give an antiemetic for the nausea.” The nausea is a symptom of the low BP (too little blood to the brain). An antiemetic treats the symptom and misses the cause.
• “Phenylephrine 100 mcg IV.” It will raise the BP, but with a heart rate of 54 the reflex slowing could make things worse. Ephedrine is the better first choice here.
• “Wait for the next BP reading.” He is telling you something is wrong now. Treat the BP you have.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after a spinal (spinal-hypotension), step 1

questions.stem:
After two doses of ephedrine the BP is 96/54, heart rate 64, and the nausea has gone. The surgeon wants to start.

The case so far: A 76-year-old man, 70 kg, with hypertension, is having a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) under spinal anaesthesia. Your consultant gave 2.5 mL of 0.5% heavy bupivacaine at L3–4. He is in lithotomy, and your consultant has gone to the control room, asking you to check the BP every 2–3 minutes. At your consultant’s request, phenylephrine and ephedrine are drawn up and labelled. Six minutes after the spinal he says, “I feel sick.” He looks pale and sweaty.

Which is the best choice?
options: Check the block height with something cold on both sides (it is at T8 on both sides), and ask about tingling or weakness in his hands and how his breathing feels.
Nothing more: the BP is better.
Tip the table head-down to bring the BP up.
questions.explain:
You need to know how high the block is. A block creeping up causes a falling BP and, if very high, trouble breathing. T8 is fine for a TURP; arm symptoms would mean a high block.

The other choices:
• “Nothing more: the BP is better.” You still don’t know how high the block is, and that tells you whether the BP is likely to fall again. Check it.
• “Tip the table head-down to bring the BP up.” Heavy bupivacaine sinks with gravity: tipping head-down in the first 20–30 minutes lets it spread higher. Raising the legs is fine; tipping the whole table isn’t.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after a spinal (spinal-hypotension), step 2

questions.stem:
Things have settled: BP 98/56, heart rate 66. The resection starts. Your consultant, back in the room, asks about fluids.

The case so far: A 76-year-old man, 70 kg, with hypertension, is having a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) under spinal anaesthesia. Your consultant gave 2.5 mL of 0.5% heavy bupivacaine at L3–4. He is in lithotomy, and your consultant has gone to the control room, asking you to check the BP every 2–3 minutes. At your consultant’s request, phenylephrine and ephedrine are drawn up and labelled. Six minutes after the spinal he says, “I feel sick.” He looks pale and sweaty.

Which is the best choice?
options: No fluid at all.

A modest fluid bolus (250–500 mL of Hartmann’s) and vasopressor boluses as needed, asking about an infusion if they keep being needed. Avoid large volumes: he is elderly, and he will also absorb some irrigation fluid.
2 L of fluid quickly.
questions.explain:
The spinal widens the vessels: vasopressors fix that better than litres of fluid. In a TURP, irrigation fluid absorbed through the prostate adds to the load.

The other choices:
• “No fluid at all.” Vasopressors are the main treatment, but a modest bolus is reasonable in a fasted elderly man. Talk it through with your consultant.
• “2 L of fluid quickly.” Too much for an elderly heart, especially with irrigation fluid being absorbed as well. Small boluses and a vasopressor.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after a spinal (spinal-hypotension), step 3

questions.stem:
Fifty minutes into a monopolar resection with glycine irrigation, he becomes restless and confused, says his vision is blurred, and feels sick again.

The case so far: A 76-year-old man, 70 kg, with hypertension, is having a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) under spinal anaesthesia. Your consultant gave 2.5 mL of 0.5% heavy bupivacaine at L3–4. He is in lithotomy, and your consultant has gone to the control room, asking you to check the BP every 2–3 minutes. At your consultant’s request, phenylephrine and ephedrine are drawn up and labelled. Six minutes after the spinal he says, “I feel sick.” He looks pale and sweaty.

Which is the best choice?
options: Suspect TURP syndrome (irrigation fluid absorbed, sodium falling): tell the surgeon to stop or finish quickly, call your consultant, give oxygen, and check sodium and glucose on a blood gas now.
Midazolam to settle him.
Phenylephrine for the nausea.
questions.explain:
Confusion, visual change, nausea, a slow heart rate and a high BP during a long resection: TURP syndrome until proven otherwise. The surgeon needs to know now.

The other choices:
• “Midazolam to settle him.” Sedation hides the cause and can obstruct his airway and slow his breathing.
• “Phenylephrine for the nausea.” His BP is high, not low: this nausea is not from a low BP. Think about what is different now.
questions.source: MO guide case: Low blood pressure after a spinal (spinal-hypotension), step 4

questions.stem:
The PACU nurse asks you about three patients. First: a 34-year-old woman, ASA 1, knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway, in PACU for 35 minutes. She is awake and chatty, moves all four limbs, breathes deeply and coughs when asked, SpO2 97% on air, BP within 10% of her pre-op value, pain 2/10, no nausea, and there were no problems in theatre.

What do you do first?
options: Only a doctor can discharge anyone after a GA.
Keep her another hour to be safe.
She meets the nurse-led discharge criteria (ASA 1–2, minor surgery, no airway or surgical problems) and her Aldrete score is 10: the nurse can discharge her.
questions.explain:
Right. ASA 1 or 2 patients after GA, regional or MAC who meet the criteria can be discharged by the nurse. Aldrete scores activity, breathing, circulation, consciousness and saturation, 0–2 each: she scores 10.

The other choices:
• “Only a doctor can discharge anyone after a GA.” At NTFGH, patients who meet the nurse-led discharge criteria can be discharged by the PACU nurse. The criteria list is in PACU.
• “Keep her another hour to be safe.” She has done her 30 minutes and meets the criteria. Keeping well patients fills PACU beds that sicker patients need.
questions.source: MO guide case: Who can leave PACU? (pacu-discharge), step 1

questions.stem:
Second: a 58-year-old man, ASA 3 (obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP, BMI 41), after a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, in PACU for 40 minutes. Awake, his SpO2 is 94% on air. When he dozes off he snores and the SpO2 falls to 88%. Pain 3/10.

The case so far: The PACU nurse asks you about three patients. First: a 34-year-old woman, ASA 1, knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway, in PACU for 35 minutes. She is awake and chatty, moves all four limbs, breathes deeply and coughs when asked, SpO2 97% on air, BP within 10% of her pre-op value, pain 2/10, no nausea, and there were no problems in theatre.

Which is the best choice?
options: He isn’t for nurse-led discharge (ASA 3, OSA, high BMI). Keep him in PACU: sit him up, give oxygen, put on his own CPAP, and discuss with the primary anaesthetist whether he needs a monitored bed.
Send him to the ward with nasal oxygen.
Nurse-led discharge: he is awake and comfortable.
questions.explain:
OSA and a high BMI are on the exclusion list. Obstruction when asleep is exactly the risk: CPAP and sitting up treat it, and a monitored bed is a senior’s decision.

The other choices:
• “Send him to the ward with nasal oxygen.” Oxygen can keep the saturation number up while he obstructs and his CO2 rises. He needs CPAP, and a senior to decide where he goes.
• “Nurse-led discharge: he is awake and comfortable.” He is excluded: ASA 3, OSA and a high BMI. And awake isn’t the test: he desaturates when asleep, which is what he will do on the ward.
questions.source: MO guide case: Who can leave PACU? (pacu-discharge), step 2

questions.stem:
On CPAP and sitting up, his SpO2 stays at 95% while asleep. The primary anaesthetist decides he should go to high dependency (HD). The nurse asks who will take him.

The case so far: The PACU nurse asks you about three patients. First: a 34-year-old woman, ASA 1, knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway, in PACU for 35 minutes. She is awake and chatty, moves all four limbs, breathes deeply and coughs when asked, SpO2 97% on air, BP within 10% of her pre-op value, pain 2/10, no nausea, and there were no problems in theatre.

Which is the best choice?
options: The primary anaesthetic team’s MO takes him to HD, and a PACU discharge note is still written.
The PACU nurse takes him alone.
You take him: you are the PACU MO.
questions.explain:
That is the department rule: HD transfers from PACU are done by the primary anaesthetic MO, and a PACU discharge note is still needed.

The other choices:
• “The PACU nurse takes him alone.” A patient going to HD goes with the primary anaesthetic MO.
• “You take him: you are the PACU MO.” The PACU MO must stay physically in PACU. HD transfers are done by the primary anaesthetic MO.
questions.source: MO guide case: Who can leave PACU? (pacu-discharge), step 3

questions.stem:
Third: a 71-year-old woman, ASA 3, after cataract surgery under topical local anaesthetic with monitoring only (MAC), given no sedation or other drugs. She has been in PACU for 10 minutes, comfortable, with normal vitals.

The case so far: The PACU nurse asks you about three patients. First: a 34-year-old woman, ASA 1, knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway, in PACU for 35 minutes. She is awake and chatty, moves all four limbs, breathes deeply and coughs when asked, SpO2 97% on air, BP within 10% of her pre-op value, pain 2/10, no nausea, and there were no problems in theatre.

Which is the best choice?
options: ASA 3, so no nurse-led discharge.

She can be fast-tracked: a stable MAC eye patient who had no drugs may leave before 30 minutes, and ASA 3 cataract patients are the one ASA 3 group allowed nurse-led discharge. The primary anaesthetist says whether fast track applies.
She must stay 30 minutes like everyone else.
questions.explain:
Right on both counts. Fast track is only for stable MAC eye cases with no medication, and the primary anaesthetist decides.

The other choices:
• “ASA 3, so no nurse-led discharge.” Cataract patients are the exception: ASA 3 cataract patients can have nurse-led discharge.
• “She must stay 30 minutes like everyone else.” Safe, but not needed. Stable MAC eye cases who had no drugs can be fast-tracked before 30 minutes if the primary anaesthetist agrees.
questions.source: MO guide case: Who can leave PACU? (pacu-discharge), step 4

questions.stem:
As the first patient stands up to leave, she says she feels faint. She is pale and sweaty.

The case so far: The PACU nurse asks you about three patients. First: a 34-year-old woman, ASA 1, knee arthroscopy under GA with a supraglottic airway, in PACU for 35 minutes. She is awake and chatty, moves all four limbs, breathes deeply and coughs when asked, SpO2 97% on air, BP within 10% of her pre-op value, pain 2/10, no nausea, and there were no problems in theatre.

Which is the best choice?
options: Give ephedrine 5 mg and let her go once the BP is up.
It’s only a faint on standing: let her go.
Stop the discharge. Lie her flat with her legs raised, recheck the BP, look at the chart and at her knee for bleeding, and give a fluid bolus. She goes only when she is stable and scores well again.
questions.explain:
A patient who met the criteria a minute ago can change. Reassess from the start: it is probably a simple faint, but rule out bleeding and drug effects first.

The other choices:
• “Give ephedrine 5 mg and let her go once the BP is up.” Treating the number and sending her off skips the question of why. Lie her down, find the cause, and discharge only when she is stable without drugs.
• “It’s only a faint on standing: let her go.” She no longer meets the discharge criteria: her BP is well below her pre-op value and she has symptoms.
questions.source: MO guide case: Who can leave PACU? (pacu-discharge), step 5

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old woman, 60 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Your consultant is doing an ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block with ropivacaine 0.5%. You inject 5 mL at a time when asked, aspirating before each. After 15 mL she says, “My lips are tingling and there’s ringing in my ears.”

What do you do first?
options: Give midazolam 2 mg for her anxiety and finish the injection.
It’s anxiety: reassure her and carry on.
Stop injecting at once and say it: “She has tingling lips and ringing ears: possible local anaesthetic toxicity.” Call for help, give 100% oxygen, and ask someone to bring the Intralipid.
questions.explain:
Exactly. Tingling lips, a metallic taste, ringing ears and light-headedness are the early warnings of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Stopping now limits the dose.

The other choices:
• “Give midazolam 2 mg for her anxiety and finish the injection.” Midazolam can hide the warning signs while you give more of the drug causing them. You finish the injection, and the toxicity gets worse.
• “It’s anxiety: reassure her and carry on.” These are classic early signs of toxicity. You inject another 10 mL, and the toxicity gets worse.
questions.source: MO guide case: Toxicity after a nerve block (last-block), step 1

questions.stem:
Thirty seconds later she stiffens and has a generalised seizure.

The case so far: A 62-year-old woman, 60 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Your consultant is doing an ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block with ropivacaine 0.5%. You inject 5 mL at a time when asked, aspirating before each. After 15 mL she says, “My lips are tingling and there’s ringing in my ears.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Give propofol 200 mg to stop the seizure.

Protect the airway and oxygenate: 100% oxygen by mask, jaw thrust, and help her breathe with the bag (high CO2 makes toxicity worse). Stop the seizure with midazolam 2–5 mg IV (repeated if needed), and get the Intralipid open.
Give suxamethonium to stop the seizure.
questions.explain:
Airway and oxygen first; a benzodiazepine for the seizure; and the antidote ready. Acidosis and high CO2 make local anaesthetic toxicity worse, so good ventilation matters.

The other choices:
• “Give propofol 200 mg to stop the seizure.” Propofol does stop seizures, but a big dose depresses a heart already poisoned by local anaesthetic. Small doses only, if at all; a benzodiazepine is preferred.
• “Give suxamethonium to stop the seizure.” It stops the movement, not the seizure in the brain, and leaves her paralysed. A benzodiazepine is the drug for the seizure. Your consultant asks for midazolam.
questions.source: MO guide case: Toxicity after a nerve block (last-block), step 2

questions.stem:
The seizure has stopped. Now the heart rate is 46, the BP 74/40, and the QRS complexes are getting wider. The Intralipid 20% arrives. How much do you give?

The case so far: A 62-year-old woman, 60 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Your consultant is doing an ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block with ropivacaine 0.5%. You inject 5 mL at a time when asked, aspirating before each. After 15 mL she says, “My lips are tingling and there’s ringing in my ears.”
options: 500 mL as fast as it will run.
Atropine, and wait to see if she recovers on her own.
A bolus of 90 mL (1.5 mL/kg) IV over 1 minute, then an infusion at 900 mL/h (15 mL/kg/h).
questions.explain:
The handbook regimen worked out for 60 kg. Write down the times and amounts: the total must not go over 12 mL/kg (720 mL for her).

The other choices:
• “500 mL as fast as it will run.” Dose by weight: a bolus of 1.5 mL/kg, then 15 mL/kg/h, with a ceiling of 12 mL/kg in total. Try again.
• “Atropine, and wait to see if she recovers on her own.” Atropine won’t reverse a heart poisoned by local anaesthetic, and every minute of waiting matters.
questions.source: MO guide case: Toxicity after a nerve block (last-block), step 3

questions.stem:
Five minutes after the bolus: heart rate 58, BP 82/46. Still low.

The case so far: A 62-year-old woman, 60 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Your consultant is doing an ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block with ropivacaine 0.5%. You inject 5 mL at a time when asked, aspirating before each. After 15 mL she says, “My lips are tingling and there’s ringing in my ears.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Stop the Intralipid: the heart rate is improving.
Repeat the 90 mL bolus (up to two repeats, 5 minutes apart), double the infusion to 1800 mL/h (30 mL/kg/h), keep the total under 720 mL, and give small vasopressor doses as your consultant directs.
Vasopressin to bring the BP up.
questions.explain:
The handbook allows the bolus to be repeated twice and the infusion doubled. If a vasopressor is needed, small doses of adrenaline (up to 1 mcg/kg) are used.

The other choices:
• “Stop the Intralipid: the heart rate is improving.” She is still hypotensive. Keep the infusion going until the circulation has been stable for at least 10 minutes, without going over the 12 mL/kg ceiling.
• “Vasopressin to bring the BP up.” Vasopressin is avoided in local anaesthetic toxicity. More Intralipid first, and small doses of adrenaline if your consultant wants a vasopressor.
questions.source: MO guide case: Toxicity after a nerve block (last-block), step 4

questions.stem:
Ten minutes later the heart rate is 84 and the BP 112/64. She is waking up and talking.

The case so far: A 62-year-old woman, 60 kg, for fixation of a broken wrist. Your consultant is doing an ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block with ropivacaine 0.5%. You inject 5 mL at a time when asked, aspirating before each. After 15 mL she says, “My lips are tingling and there’s ringing in my ears.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Keep her monitored in high dependency (HD) or the ICU for at least 4–6 hours, postpone the surgery (your consultant decides), record the drug, dose and timings, report the event, and explain to her what happened.
Send her back to the ward.
Carry on with the surgery under GA now that she is stable.
questions.explain:
Toxicity can come back as the Intralipid wears off: at least 2 hours of monitoring after a seizure alone, 4–6 hours after any heart effects, as here. Postponing is usual, and an honest explanation is part of the care. Lipid can cause pancreatitis, so amylase or lipase is checked for two days.

The other choices:
• “Send her back to the ward.” She needs monitoring for several hours in HD or ICU, because toxicity can come back.
• “Carry on with the surgery under GA now that she is stable.” She has just had a seizure and heart effects from toxicity, and can relapse. The operation isn’t urgent: your consultant will almost certainly postpone it.
questions.source: MO guide case: Toxicity after a nerve block (last-block), step 5

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old man, 110 kg, 175 cm (BMI 36), for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Mallampati 3, thick neck. Your consultant induced with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium after showing that mask ventilation was easy. Their third attempt at intubation, with a video laryngoscope and a bougie, has just failed. SpO2 91%. Your consultant: “Can’t get it.”

What do you do first?
options: Offer to try yourself.
Start drawing up sugammadex so he can be woken.
Say “Failed intubation”. Call for more help, bring the difficult airway trolley, and hand over a second-generation supraglottic airway (an i-gel size 5), with face-mask oxygen meanwhile.
questions.explain:
Saying “failed intubation” moves everyone to plan B: oxygenate with a supraglottic airway. Getting more help and the trolley are jobs you can do straight away.

The other choices:
• “Offer to try yourself.” After three failed attempts by your consultant, more attempts (especially by someone less experienced) cause swelling and bleeding and can turn “can oxygenate” into “can’t”. Move to plan B.
• “Start drawing up sugammadex so he can be woken.” Waking him up may well be the plan, and sugammadex for a 110 kg man takes several vials, so starting it is useful. But oxygen comes first: someone must also call for help and pass the supraglottic airway. Your consultant asks the nurse for the i-gel.
questions.source: MO guide case: Failed intubation (cant-intubate), step 1

questions.stem:
Your consultant inserts an i-gel size 5. There is a square capnography trace, the chest rises and the SpO2 climbs to 96%. Your consultant: “OK. Stop and think. What are our options?”

The case so far: A 50-year-old man, 110 kg, 175 cm (BMI 36), for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Mallampati 3, thick neck. Your consultant induced with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium after showing that mask ventilation was easy. Their third attempt at intubation, with a video laryngoscope and a bougie, has just failed. SpO2 91%. Your consultant: “Can’t get it.”

Which is the best choice?
options: Carry on with the surgery using the i-gel.
Take out the i-gel and try once more with a laryngoscope.

Wake him up: it is an elective operation. Sugammadex 16 mg/kg (1760 mg for 110 kg) as your consultant decides, turn off the anaesthetic, keep oxygenating through the i-gel, and plan the next anaesthetic differently.
questions.explain:
For elective surgery, waking up is usually the safest answer once you can oxygenate. Sugammadex 16 mg/kg reverses rocuronium within about 3 minutes; at 100 mg/mL that is about 18 mL from several vials. It removes the relaxant but doesn’t open a swollen or obstructed airway, so keep oxygenating.

The other choices:
• “Carry on with the surgery using the i-gel.” For an elective laparoscopic operation, with gas in the abdomen and a raised risk of regurgitation, carrying on with a supraglottic airway is rarely right. It is reserved for life-saving surgery, and it is the consultant’s call.
• “Take out the i-gel and try once more with a laryngoscope.” You have just rescued oxygenation. Removing the device that works, for a fourth attempt, risks losing the airway completely.
questions.source: MO guide case: Failed intubation (cant-intubate), step 2

questions.stem:
Within 2 minutes of the sugammadex the TOF ratio is over 0.9; he breathes strongly and wakes up. Your consultant takes the i-gel out once he is awake. What now?

The case so far: A 50-year-old man, 110 kg, 175 cm (BMI 36), for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Mallampati 3, thick neck. Your consultant induced with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium after showing that mask ventilation was easy. Their third attempt at intubation, with a video laryngoscope and a bougie, has just failed. SpO2 91%. Your consultant: “Can’t get it.”
options: Help your consultant record exactly what happened (the Cormack–Lehane grade of each view, devices, attempts, that mask ventilation was easy, what worked), explain it to him once he is awake, and make sure there is a difficult airway alert in his records and a letter for him and his family doctor.
Just write “difficult intubation” in the notes.
Don’t tell him: it would worry him.
questions.explain:
The next anaesthetist’s plan depends on what you write today. An alert and a letter mean he will be planned for properly, probably with an awake intubation.

The other choices:
• “Just write “difficult intubation” in the notes.” Not enough. The next team needs the details: views, devices tried, number of attempts, what worked, and whether mask ventilation was easy.
• “Don’t tell him: it would worry him.” He needs to know, and to tell every future anaesthetist. Explain it plainly once he is awake.
questions.source: MO guide case: Failed intubation (cant-intubate), step 3

questions.stem:
A fit 30-year-old woman, 58 kg, for a diagnostic laparoscopy under GA with a tracheal tube. Your consultant has stepped out to the control room. As the surgeon starts insufflating CO2, the heart rate falls from 72 to 35.

What do you do first?
options: Tell the surgeon clearly: “Heart rate 35: please stop and let the gas out.” Ask the nurse to call your consultant.
Give atropine first, without disturbing the surgeon.
Wait: it usually settles by itself.
questions.explain:
Stretching the peritoneum triggers a vagal reflex. Removing the trigger is the fastest fix, and the surgeon can only stop if you tell them, loudly.

The other choices:
• “Give atropine first, without disturbing the surgeon.” Atropine helps, but stopping the stretch (the trigger) is faster and more reliable. Tell the surgeon at the same time.
• “Wait: it usually settles by itself.” It may settle, but it may also slow further to asystole. Act now.
questions.source: MO guide case: Bradycardia when the gas goes in (brady-pneumoperitoneum), step 1

questions.stem:
The surgeon lets the gas out. Heart rate 48, BP 86/48.

The case so far: A fit 30-year-old woman, 58 kg, for a diagnostic laparoscopy under GA with a tracheal tube. Your consultant has stepped out to the control room. As the surgeon starts insufflating CO2, the heart rate falls from 72 to 35.

Which is the best choice?
options: Atropine 0.1 mg IV.
Atropine 0.6 mg IV (1 mL of 600 mcg/mL).
Glycopyrrolate 0.2–0.4 mg IV.
questions.explain:
Atropine blocks the vagal effect within a minute.

The other choices:
• “Atropine 0.1 mg IV.” Too small: in adults, very small doses (under about 0.3 mg) can briefly slow the heart further. For a sudden vagal bradycardia give 0.6 mg (one ampoule).
• “Glycopyrrolate 0.2–0.4 mg IV.” It works too, but more slowly than atropine. It suits slower, less urgent bradycardia.
questions.source: MO guide case: Bradycardia when the gas goes in (brady-pneumoperitoneum), step 2

questions.stem:
Heart rate 84, BP 112/66. The surgeon wants to start again.

The case so far: A fit 30-year-old woman, 58 kg, for a diagnostic laparoscopy under GA with a tracheal tube. Your consultant has stepped out to the control room. As the surgeon starts insufflating CO2, the heart rate falls from 72 to 35.

Which is the best choice?
options: Ask the surgeon to convert to an open operation.
Agree, but ask for slow insufflation to a lower pressure (for example 12 mmHg). Keep atropine ready, watch the ECG, and tell the surgeon at once if the rate drops.
Ask them to insufflate fast to get it over with.
questions.explain:
Slow, low-pressure insufflation rarely triggers the reflex again, and you are ready if it does.

The other choices:
• “Ask the surgeon to convert to an open operation.” Not needed: this is a common reflex that rarely recurs with slow insufflation. If it kept happening, your consultant and the surgeon would decide.
• “Ask them to insufflate fast to get it over with.” Fast stretching is what triggered it. Slow and low is the way.
questions.source: MO guide case: Bradycardia when the gas goes in (brady-pneumoperitoneum), step 3

questions.stem:
Insufflation is complete at 12 mmHg, with her tilted head-down for the pelvis. Twenty minutes later the EtCO2 has climbed to 52 mmHg and the peak airway pressure is 30 cmH2O.

The case so far: A fit 30-year-old woman, 58 kg, for a diagnostic laparoscopy under GA with a tracheal tube. Your consultant has stepped out to the control room. As the surgeon starts insufflating CO2, the heart rate falls from 72 to 35.

Which is the best choice?
options: Ignore it: CO2 always rises in laparoscopy.

Increase the breathing rate to clear the absorbed CO2, check the tube hasn’t slipped deeper with the head-down tilt (listen to both sides), feel for crackling under the skin (surgical emphysema), and tell your consultant.
Give sodium bicarbonate for the acid.
questions.explain:
CO2 is absorbed from the abdomen, so the minute ventilation needs to go up. The gas and the head-down tilt push the diaphragm and the lungs up towards the head while the tube stays fixed at the teeth, so its tip can end up in a bronchus, which raises the pressure too.

The other choices:
• “Ignore it: CO2 always rises in laparoscopy.” Some rise is expected, but you treat it, and you look for causes that need action.
• “Give sodium bicarbonate for the acid.” The acid comes from CO2, which leaves through the lungs. Breathe more for her instead.
questions.source: MO guide case: Bradycardia when the gas goes in (brady-pneumoperitoneum), step 4
